title: Can you make a class `private` (only nested classes, not top-level) and why?
shortTitle: Can you make a class private?

s1_definition.profdef: A top-level class cannot be declared `private`; the only legal access modifiers on a top-level class are `public` or package-private, which is the default when no modifier is written. A nested class, however, can be `private`, `protected`, `public`, or package-private, because a nested class is a member of its enclosing class and members may carry any access level. A private nested class is visible only inside its enclosing class, which is useful for implementation details that must never leak out.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India head office. A top-level class is like a whole branch building; it cannot be truly private because at the very least the postal service in its own area, meaning other classes in the same package, must be able to find it. But inside a branch, the manager can keep a locked drawer, a private nested class, that only he and his own office can open. Nobody outside that office even knows the drawer exists. So privacy at the drawer level is allowed, but a whole building cannot be hidden from its own neighborhood.
s1_definition.oneliner: Only nested classes can be private because they are members of an enclosing class; a top-level class can only be public or package-private.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A top-level class cannot be declared `private`; the only legal access modifiers on a top-level class are `public` or package-private, which is the default when no modifier is written. A nested class, however, can be `private`, `protected`, `public`, or package-private, because a nested class is a member of its enclosing class and members may carry any access level. A private nested class is visible only inside its enclosing class, which is useful for implementation details that must never leak out.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India head office. A top-level class is like a whole branch building; it cannot be truly private because at the very least the postal service in its own area, meaning other classes in the same package, must be able to find it. But inside a branch, the manager can keep a locked drawer, a private nested class, that only he and his own office can open. Nobody outside that office even knows the drawer exists. So privacy at the drawer level is allowed, but a whole building cannot be hidden from its own neighborhood.

**One line to remember:** Only nested classes can be private because they are members of an enclosing class; a top-level class can only be public or package-private.

sections.s2_technical:
The Java language specification restricts the modifiers allowed on a top-level class to `public` and nothing. If you write `private class Account {}` at the top level of a file, the compiler rejects it with an error like "modifier private not allowed here." The reason is that access modifiers describe visibility relative to some enclosing scope, and a top-level class's enclosing scope is its package. The two meaningful visibilities there are public, meaning visible everywhere, and package-private, meaning visible only within the same package. A hypothetical private top-level class would be visible to nothing, not even itself in a useful way, so the language simply forbids it.

A nested class is different because it is a member of its enclosing class, exactly like a field or method, and members can carry all four access levels. So `private static class Node {}` inside a `LinkedLedger` class is perfectly legal and is visible only within `LinkedLedger`. This is extremely common in the standard library; for example, HashMap has a private static Node class and a private static TreeNode class that callers never see. A small banking usage is a private static helper inside a service: `private static class TransferAttempt { final BigDecimal amount; int retries; }` used only by that service's internal retry logic.

Why would you want a private nested class? The main reason is to hide implementation detail completely. If a type exists only to support one enclosing class and should never be referenced from anywhere else, marking it private enforces that at compile time, so no other code can ever depend on it. This keeps your public surface area small, which is the heart of good encapsulation. A protected or package-private nested class offers intermediate visibility, for example a nested class that subclasses or same-package test code may use but the wider world may not.

The senior nuance is the distinction between a top-level class with default (package-private) access and a nested private class. People sometimes say they want a private class when they really mean package-private, which hides the class from other packages but still allows the same package to use it. Also, a private nested class can still be reached reflectively, and the compiler historically generated synthetic accessor methods for private members accessed across the nest boundary, though since Java 11 the nestmates feature lets nested and enclosing classes access each other's private members directly without synthetic bridges, which is cleaner and slightly faster.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer service retries a failed transfer a few times, and to track each attempt it needs a small object holding the amount and a retry counter. This object is meaningless outside the service and must never be used by other code. This is exactly what a private nested class is for, because marking it private guarantees at compile time that nothing outside the service can reference it.

Problem 2 — A developer tried to declare that helper as a private top-level class in its own file and the code would not compile. This demonstrates the rule that a top-level class can only be public or package-private, never private, so the helper had to become a private nested class inside the service instead.

In the mini-project we build a `TransferService` with a private static nested `TransferAttempt` class and show that moving the same class to the top level with the private modifier is a compile error (shown as a commented-out block). The demo transfers between Rajesh and Priya with retry tracking, logging each attempt.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/privateclass/PrivateClassDemo.java
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh at 1,000,000 and Priya at 250,000, a transfer of 50,000 with up to three retries.

Step 1: Main creates a `TransferService` and calls `transferWithRetry`. The accounts are passed in; nothing has changed yet.

Step 2: Inside the service, a private nested `TransferAttempt` is created holding the amount and a retry counter of zero. This object exists only within the service and cannot be referenced from main.

Step 3: The loop checks Rajesh's balance against the amount. He has enough, so it debits him to 950,000 and credits Priya to 300,000, logs success on attempt one, and returns true.

Step 4: Control returns to main, which logs the final balances. The TransferAttempt object has already gone out of scope and is unreachable, and because it is private, no other class ever saw its type.

```text
[INFO] transfer succeeded on attempt 1
[INFO] Transfer success=true rajesh=Rs.950000 priya=Rs.300000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  main (PrivateClassDemo)
    │ transferWithRetry(rajesh, priya, 50,000, 3)
    ▼
  TransferService  (package-private top-level — CANNOT be private)
    │ new TransferAttempt(50,000)   ← PRIVATE NESTED, invisible outside
    │ retries=0
    ├─ balance 1,000,000 >= 50,000 ? YES
    │     debit  → 950,000
    │     credit → 300,000
    │     return true
    ▼
  main logs final balances
  (TransferAttempt type never escapes the service)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Class Access Levels ═══

  ┌─ Rule ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TOP-LEVEL class: public | package-private (default)   │
  │   → private / protected NOT allowed                   │
  │ NESTED class (member): public | protected |           │
  │   package-private | private  → ALL four allowed       │
  │ Encapsulation (SRP + information hiding):              │
  │   private nested = impl detail, no external coupling   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TransferService (package-private)      │
  │  + transferWithRetry(..):boolean       │  public surface
  │                                        │
  │  ┌── private static nested ────────┐   │
  │  │ TransferAttempt                 │   │  visible ONLY here
  │  │ - amount:BigDecimal             │   │
  │  │ - retries:int                   │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  Compile error example (top level):
    private class X {}   // "modifier private not allowed here"

  Nestmates (Java 11+): enclosing & nested share private
  access directly, no synthetic bridge methods.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, you cannot make a top-level class private. The Java language only allows two access levels on a top-level class: public, meaning visible everywhere, or package-private, which is the default you get when you write no modifier at all and which makes the class visible only within its own package. If you try to write the word private in front of a top-level class, the compiler rejects it with an error saying the private modifier is not allowed there. The reason is that access modifiers express visibility relative to an enclosing scope, and the enclosing scope of a top-level class is its package, where the only sensible choices are public or package-private. A truly private top-level class would be visible to nothing, so the language forbids it.

A nested class is a completely different situation, because a nested class is a member of its enclosing class in exactly the same way a field or a method is, and members are allowed to carry all four access levels. So a private nested class is perfectly legal, and it is visible only inside its enclosing class. This pattern is everywhere in the standard library: HashMap, for example, has a private static Node class and a private static TreeNode class that callers can never see or name.

The reason I use a private nested class is to hide an implementation detail completely. In my banking transfer service I needed a tiny helper to track each retry attempt, holding the amount and a retry counter, and that helper has no meaning anywhere outside the service. By making it a private static nested class, I guarantee at compile time that no other code can ever reference it, which keeps the public surface of the service small and prevents any outside coupling to an internal detail. When I first wrote that helper as a private top-level class in its own file it would not compile, which is exactly the rule in action, so it became a private nested class instead.

The senior nuance I add is that people often say private when they actually mean package-private. Package-private hides a class from other packages while still letting the same package use it, which is the right choice for classes that collaborate within a module but should not be part of the public API. And since Java 11, the nestmates feature lets an enclosing class and its nested classes access each other's private members directly, without the synthetic accessor bridge methods the compiler used to generate, which makes private nested classes both cleaner and marginally faster.

---

keyPoints: Top-level class: cannot be private (only public or package-private)
Inner class: can be private — visible only inside the enclosing class
Private inner class is a common encapsulation pattern
Example: private Node class inside LinkedList
